subject: history
topicDisplay: Stuart Britain The Crisis Of Monarchy 1603 1702
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The set of laws passed 1661-65 to enforce Anglican conformity and penalise dissenters was the:
questions.explain: The Clarendon Code, a series of Restoration statutes, enforced Anglican uniformity and restricted Protestant Dissenters.

questions.q: The professional Parliamentarian army created by ordinance in 1645 was called the:
questions.explain: The New Model Army, formed in 1645 and commanded by Fairfax, was a disciplined national force pivotal to Parliament's victory.

questions.q: The 1644 parliamentary and Scottish victory in the north was the Battle of:
questions.explain: The Battle of Marston Moor (July 1644) was a major Parliamentarian-Scottish victory that secured the north of England.

questions.q: The 1701 Act of Settlement secured the Protestant succession by vesting the crown in the House of:
questions.explain: The Act of Settlement (1701) settled the succession on Sophia of Hanover and her Protestant heirs, leading to the Hanoverian succession in 1714.

questions.q: The purge of Parliament in December 1648 that removed members opposed to trying the king was carried out by:
questions.explain: Pride's Purge (December 1648) expelled MPs unwilling to try Charles I, leaving the Rump Parliament to proceed.

questions.q: Charles II set out his conditions for returning to the throne in the 1660 document called the:
questions.explain: The Declaration of Breda (1660) promised pardons, religious toleration and arrears of pay, smoothing Charles II's Restoration.

questions.q: James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, founding which royal dynasty in England?
questions.explain: On Elizabeth I's death in 1603 James VI of Scotland acceded as James I, beginning the Stuart dynasty in England.

questions.q: The 1670 secret treaty in which Charles II promised to convert to Catholicism in return for French money was the Treaty of:
questions.explain: The secret Treaty of Dover (1670) bound Charles II to Louis XIV, including a pledge to declare himself Catholic.

questions.q: The 1685 rebellion against James II led by Charles II's illegitimate son ended at the Battle of Sedgemoor; its leader was:
questions.explain: The Duke of Monmouth's 1685 rebellion was crushed at Sedgemoor, followed by the savage 'Bloody Assizes'.

questions.q: Who succeeded Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector on his death in 1658?
questions.explain: Richard Cromwell briefly succeeded his father in 1658 but lacked authority and resigned in 1659.

questions.q: James II's 1687 and 1688 Declarations of Indulgence aimed to grant toleration to:
questions.explain: James II's Declarations of Indulgence suspended penal laws against both Catholics and Dissenters, alarming the Anglican establishment.

questions.q: Charles I's Archbishop of Canterbury, whose religious reforms provoked Puritan anger, was:
questions.explain: William Laud's emphasis on ceremony and uniformity ('Laudianism') alienated Puritans and helped spark conflict.

questions.q: The 1673 Test Act required office-holders to do what, exposing the Catholicism of James, Duke of York?
options: Take Anglican communion and renounce transubstantiation
questions.explain: The Test Act (1673) required officials to take Anglican communion, forcing James to resign as Lord High Admiral and revealing his faith.

questions.q: James II acceded to the throne in which year?
questions.explain: James II succeeded his brother Charles II in February 1685, the first openly Catholic monarch since Mary I.

questions.q: The 1610 financial scheme proposed by Robert Cecil to reform royal finances was called the:
questions.explain: The Great Contract of 1610 proposed exchanging feudal dues for a fixed parliamentary income, but it collapsed without agreement.

questions.q: In which year was the monarchy restored with Charles II returning to England?
questions.explain: Charles II returned to England in May 1660, restoring the Stuart monarchy after the Interregnum.

questions.q: Charles I acceded to the throne in which year?
questions.explain: Charles I succeeded his father James I in 1625, soon clashing with Parliament over finance, religion and prerogative.

questions.q: The fabricated 1678 conspiracy alleging a Catholic plan to kill Charles II was the:
questions.explain: Titus Oates's fictitious Popish Plot (1678) unleashed anti-Catholic hysteria and helped trigger the Exclusion Crisis.

questions.q: The 1641 parliamentary list of grievances against Charles I's government was the:
questions.explain: The Grand Remonstrance of 1641 catalogued Charles I's misgovernment, deepening the split between king and Parliament.

questions.q: The 1657 document that offered Cromwell the crown (which he declined) was the:
questions.explain: The Humble Petition and Advice (1657) offered Cromwell the crown; he refused but accepted enhanced powers.

questions.q: The 1605 plot to blow up Parliament and King James I is known as the:
questions.explain: The Gunpowder Plot of November 1605, involving Guy Fawkes and Catholic conspirators, aimed to destroy King and Parliament.

questions.q: In which year did the First English Civil War begin when Charles I raised his standard at Nottingham?
questions.explain: Charles I raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642, marking the outbreak of the First English Civil War.

questions.q: Cromwell's 1650 victory over the Scots, who had proclaimed Charles II king, was at the Battle of:
questions.explain: At Dunbar (September 1650) Cromwell defeated a larger Scottish army that had allied with Charles II.

questions.q: Which non-parliamentary tax, extended inland by Charles I, was challenged by John Hampden in 1637?
questions.explain: Ship money, traditionally a coastal levy, was controversially extended inland and challenged by John Hampden in 1637.

questions.q: Charles I ruled without summoning Parliament during a period known as the:
questions.explain: From 1629 to 1640 Charles I governed without Parliament, a period called the Personal Rule or 'Eleven Years' Tyranny'.

questions.q: The first major pitched battle of the Civil War in October 1642 was the:
questions.explain: The Battle of Edgehill (October 1642) was the first major engagement of the Civil War and proved indecisive.

questions.q: In 1653 Cromwell forcibly dissolved which body before becoming Lord Protector?
questions.explain: Cromwell expelled the Rump Parliament in April 1653, leading to Barebone's Parliament and then the Protectorate.

questions.q: The 1679-81 political crisis over barring the Catholic James from the succession is known as the:
questions.explain: The Exclusion Crisis (1679-81) saw attempts to exclude James, Duke of York from the throne, giving rise to Whigs and Tories.

questions.q: The 1651 battle that finally ended Charles II's bid for the throne and the Civil Wars was the Battle of:
questions.explain: The Battle of Worcester (September 1651) crushed Charles II's army, after which he fled abroad into exile.

questions.q: The written constitution under which Cromwell became Lord Protector in December 1653 was the:
questions.explain: The Instrument of Government (1653) was England's first written constitution, establishing Cromwell as Lord Protector.
